hints: Start by identifying each structure: which N is directly attached to the ring, which is separated by a $\text{CH}_2$ group, and which is next to a $\text{C=O}$ group, then think about how available each nitrogen lone pair is to accept $\text{H}^+$.

Recall what happens to the nitrogen lone pair in phenylamine when it can overlap with the pi system of the benzene ring, compared to phenylmethanamine where a $\text{CH}_2$ spacer blocks that overlap.
Consider the extra effect of the carbonyl oxygen in benzamide on the nitrogen lone pair and why amides are effectively neutral rather than basic.
walkthrough:
Picture basicity as lone pair availability**
Think of a base as a lone pair donor to $\text{H}^+$. All three compounds have a nitrogen with a lone pair: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$ (S, benzamide), $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ (T, phenylamine) and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ (U, phenylmethanamine). The more localised and electron rich that lone pair is, the stronger the base.

Compare U and T, the spacer makes all the difference**
In T the nitrogen is bonded directly to the ring, so its p orbital overlaps with the delocalised pi system. Its lone pair is partly drawn into the ring and is less free to bond to $\text{H}^+$. In U the $\text{CH}_2$ group sits between the ring and the nitrogen. That breaks the overlap, so the lone pair stays localised on N. Added to that, the alkyl $\text{CH}_2$ group pushes electron density toward N, making the lone pair even more ready to accept a proton. So U is more basic than T.

See why the amide S is weakest**
In S the nitrogen is next to $\text{C=O}$. The lone pair on N is strongly delocalised onto the very electronegative oxygen to give $\text{C-O}^-$ and $\text{C=N}^+$ character. The electron withdrawing carbonyl group leaves almost no electron density on N to donate to $\text{H}^+$. That is why amides are neutral and far less basic than amines. Putting it together: U > T > S.

Final answer: U most basic > T > S least basic
phenylmethanamine / U > phenylamine / T > benzamide / S
In U the alkyl $\text{CH}_2$ group is electron donating so the N lone pair is localised and readily available to accept a proton.
In T the N lone pair overlaps with / is delocalised into the benzene pi system so is less available to accept a proton.
In S the electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$ / carbonyl group withdraws the N lone pair, delocalising it onto oxygen, so it is essentially unavailable, amides are neutral.

hints: Look at reaction 1: the $\text{C=O}$ of an amide becomes $\text{CH}_2$ in an amine, so focus on which powerful hydride reducing agent is needed for amides.

Look at reaction 2: $\text{C-Br}$ becomes $\text{C-NH}_2$, so think about what nitrogen nucleophile in excess, with what heating condition to prevent further substitution, converts a bromoalkane to a primary amine.
walkthrough:
Recognise amide to amine as reduction**
Reaction 1 converts $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Oxygen is lost and hydrogen is gained at carbon, so the carbonyl is reduced to $\text{CH}_2$. Amides are very resistant, $\text{NaBH}_4$ or $\text{H}_2$/Ni will not do it. You need lithium aluminium hydride, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$, followed by aqueous work up.

Recognise bromoalkane to amine as ammonolysis**
Reaction 2 converts $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. This is $\text{NH}_3$ acting as a nucleophile to displace $\text{Br}^-$. Use excess concentrated ammonia heated under pressure, or in a sealed tube, so the initial primary amine product is favoured and does not react further to secondary and tertiary amines.

Final answer: reaction 1: $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$
reaction 2: heat $\text{NH}_{3}$ under pressure / heat $\text{NH}_{3}$ in a sealed tube

hints: For reaction 1, think about the general class that describes gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen at carbon when $\text{C=O}$ becomes $\text{CH}_2$.
For reaction 2, think about the role of $\text{NH}_3$ as an electron pair donor attacking carbon and displacing $\text{Br}^-$, and what that substitution mechanism is called.
walkthrough:
Classify reaction 1**
The transformation $\text{RCONH}_2$ to $\text{RCH}_2\text{NH}_2$ involves removal of O and addition of H, with no change in carbon skeleton. That is the definition of reduction, here hydride reduction of the carbonyl.

Name the mechanism of reaction 2**
$\text{NH}_3$ uses its lone pair to attack the electron deficient carbon of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, $\text{Br}^-$ leaves. A nucleophile replaces a leaving group at a saturated carbon, so the mechanism is nucleophilic substitution.

Final answer: type of reaction in reaction 1: reduction
mechanism of reaction 2: nucleophilic substitution
